title: Hackers reveal how Flock cameras really track cars and people
gist: A hacker collective calling itself stegan0gram physically removed a Flock Safety license plate reader, copied its storage and recovered an on-device encryption key that unlocked thousands of vehicle detection videos, which they shared with 404 Media and WIRED. Analysis shows the camera runs about 20 Flock-built Android apps that explicitly detect people as well as vehicles and bicycles, generated roughly 1.6 million images from ~50,200 vehicles over 21 days of logs, and sometimes mis-cropped bumper stickers and an American flag patch as license plates.

themes.theme: The breach and what it exposed

insights.claim: Hackers pulled down a Flock camera above a roadway, made a near-complete copy of the data stored inside it, and shared the files with 404 Media, the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, and WIRED for a joint investigation.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Physical device capture is becoming a journalism-adjacent method for auditing opaque surveillance vendors.
insights.locator: Hackers ripped down a Flock camera above a roadway

insights.claim: The hackers accessed the camera's Android system and found several unencrypted partitions, including one called 'vendor' and another called 'media' — the latter containing an encryption key that unlocked the partition holding much of the videos and stills.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Storing the decryption key in an unencrypted partition on the same device defeats the purpose of on-device encryption.
insights.locator: The hackers said they were able to access the Android system on the camera

insights.claim: The breach undercuts Flock's description of its system as protected by on-device encryption, though much of the most sensitive storage remained encrypted and inaccessible to the researchers.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Vendor security claims about edge devices deserve independent verification, not acceptance at face value.
insights.locator: The breach provides an unprecedented look inside a system

insights.claim: In early 2025 security researcher Jon 'GainSec' Gaines reverse-engineered a Flock license plate reader and documented flaws enabling root access; Flock acknowledged but downplayed them, arguing the flaws required physical access and that an attacker 'would still not be able to gain access to footage' because images stayed on the device only briefly.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The new dump directly contradicts the vendor's earlier dismissal — a documented case of a downplayed vulnerability proving material.
insights.quote: would still not be able to gain access to footage
insights.locator: In early 2025, security researcher Jon “GainSec” Gaines

insights.claim: A Flock spokesperson responded that 'the unauthorized removal and tampering of a Flock camera is illegal' and said the company received no report through its public Vulnerability Disclosure Policy and lacks enough detail to assess the claims.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The company's framing shifts focus to the legality of the method rather than the substance of the findings.
insights.quote: The unauthorized removal and tampering of a Flock camera is illegal.
insights.locator: A Flock spokesperson said in a statement

insights.claim: The software running on the camera explicitly detects people as well as vehicles, license plates and bicycles, recording where a person appears in the image and how confident it is in the detection — a capability typically overlooked in discussions about Flock cameras.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Person detection turns a 'license plate reader' into a general people-tracking sensor, which changes the civil-liberties calculus entirely.
insights.locator: The software running on the camera explicitly detects people

insights.claim: WIRED extracted the detection models from the camera's files and ran them against test images, finding they readily detected people including a selfie of a reporter, and across 27,321 short video clips the models detected people in 11 clips, all motorcyclists — a low count attributed to the camera pointing down at roadway traffic where pedestrians rarely appear.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The capability is real and only the camera's placement limits it — relocate the camera and the people-tracking scales.
insights.locator: To test what the software could actually see

insights.claim: The camera's license plate detector sometimes mistook bumper stickers, dealership frames and other graphics for plates and cropped them out as if they were plates, including an American flag patch on a motorcyclist's saddlebag.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: False-positive cropping means the system inadvertently collects political and personal expression, not just plate numbers.
insights.locator: The tests also showed how broadly the camera’s license plate detector could interpret

insights.claim: Flock insists its cameras do not perform face recognition, and WIRED and 404 Media found no evidence of face-recognition capabilities beyond those included by default in Android, which did not appear enabled or in active use.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A vendor claim that independently checked out — useful for calibrating which Flock denials to trust.
insights.locator: Flock insists its cameras do not perform face recognition

insights.claim: The device's processor is similar to those in midrange smartphones and it runs about 20 Flock-built apps handling motion detection, photography, object classification, data upload and remote updates.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Commodity smartphone-class hardware means the per-unit cost of mass surveillance deployment is low.
insights.locator: The device’s processor is similar to those used in midrange smartphones

insights.claim: When something moves into view the camera takes a rapid burst of photos — a typical passing vehicle generates about 28 images, with some producing more than 100 — using different exposures to capture both the plate and the wider scene before cropping and uploading over cellular.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Dozens of images per vehicle means far more visual context is captured than a 'plate read' implies.
insights.locator: According to the code, when something moves into view

insights.claim: The camera itself does not appear to read the plate or identify vehicle make, model and color; that processing appears to happen on Flock's servers.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Server-side inference means Flock, not the local agency, controls what attributes are extracted and retained.
insights.locator: The camera itself does not appear to read the plate

insights.claim: Across about 21 days of recoverable logs the single device photographed roughly 50,200 vehicles and generated about 1.6 million images, averaging around 3,300 vehicles a day with a high of 4,454.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A concrete per-camera throughput figure that lets anyone estimate the data volume of a citywide deployment.
insights.locator: the camera’s logs recorded about 21 days of activity

insights.claim: The camera's logs show it struggling with storage, recording more than 27,000 'no space left on device' errors while trying to save full-resolution images, plus tens of thousands of related errors, crashes and reboots.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Operational fragility at the edge suggests real-world data capture is lossier than marketing implies.
insights.locator: The camera’s logs also show the camera struggling with storage

insights.claim: Roughly every two minutes a watchdog process logged the message 'Who's a good boy?!' — appearing more than 12,000 times in recovered logs — and on restart another service logged 'A reboot was requested! ¡Adiós, Amigos!'
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A small humanizing detail that also confirms the researchers had genuine access to internal logs.
insights.locator: about every two minutes, code checked that the camera was still running

themes.theme: The national network and its misuse

insights.claim: Flock makes time-stamped vehicle records searchable not just by the local agency that owns the cameras but by police departments nationwide through the company's national network.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Local procurement decisions silently grant nationwide access — the key structural feature driving the controversy.
insights.locator: But in many cases, Flock’s system also allows other police departments

insights.claim: In Alpharetta, Georgia, WIRED found records from city Flock cameras were accessible to more than 2,000 agencies including police departments, colleges, airports and, inexplicably, the Office of Inspector General for the federal General Services Administration.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A quantified access footprint of one small city's cameras — the clearest illustration of scope creep.
insights.locator: In Alpharetta, Georgia, for example

insights.claim: 404 Media revealed that local police performed national-network lookups on behalf of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including in jurisdictions that had banned working with immigration authorities or transferring license plate data out of state, and that a Texas officer searched Flock cameras nationwide for a woman who self-administered an abortion.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that local legal restrictions are routed around via a private national database — the precedent that fuels the backlash.
insights.locator: 404 Media revealed that local cops were performing lookups

insights.claim: In August WIRED obtained frontend code for Flock's police software — now called OS Investigate, previously Nightshift — and reconstructed portions showing it can combine camera records with police files and commercial data to identify drivers, surface vehicles that repeatedly travel together, and search for people based on patterns of movement.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Co-travel and movement-pattern search is association mapping, a far more invasive capability than plate lookup.
insights.locator: In August, WIRED obtained frontend code for Flock’s police software

insights.claim: Multiple people across the country have been arrested for allegedly tampering with or sabotaging Flock cameras, some towns have announced they will stop using Flock entirely, and one police department made a fake 3D-printed Flock camera case to bait vandals.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Physical resistance plus municipal cancellations are becoming a real commercial risk factor for surveillance vendors.
insights.locator: Across the country, multiple people have been arrested

insights.claim: A member of the stegan0gram collective framed the operation as an escalation from destruction to intelligence gathering, saying 'Why just destroy them when we can reverse engineer them and find the secrets of those spying on us?' and describing the act as liberating and disarming hardware in the field.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Signals a shift in activist tactics from vandalism toward technical disclosure — a more durable threat to vendors.
insights.quote: Why just destroy them when we can reverse engineer them and find the secrets of those spying on us?
insights.locator: one of the hackers, from a collective calling itself stegan0gram, said

insights.claim: The hackers say they are also publishing details of how they obtained the software in the hope that others will copy them, and acknowledged that 'being investigated is a legit concern' they are trying to avoid.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Published methodology means further camera dumps are likely — expect more disclosures on the same model.
insights.quote: Being investigated is a legit concern and something we are trying to avoid.
insights.locator: One of the hackers said

insights.claim: Noel Pichardo, a former Pawtucket, Rhode Island police officer and Flock critic, warns that sabotage may backfire: 'I think that type of vigilantism will only crystallize the police and the state at large in their belief that this tool is necessary.'
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive second-order effect: activist destruction may strengthen the procurement case it aims to defeat.
insights.quote: The longer the state continues to ignore the groanings of their constituents who are against this type of surveillance, the more this will happen.
insights.locator: Pichardo says
